articles.title: India-China border face-offs test Modi six years after deadly clash
articles.summary: Despite thaw in India-China ties, border tensions again challenge Modi’s strongman image at home.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – India’s armed forces are locked in multiple ongoing face-offs with the Chinese army along the border in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, the chief of India’s paramilitary border force guarding the Himalayan frontier with China has said.

The remarks late last week by Shatrujeet Kapur, the director-general of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) paramilitary force, come nearly four months after local civil society groups in the remote northeastern region told Al Jazeera that Chinese forces were increasingly encroaching on Indian territory and denying Indian troops access to patrolling points, angering locals.

Chinese President Xi Jinping was in New Delhi last month – his first trip to India in seven years – for the BRICS summit, where he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines, as the two capitals pursued a cautious thaw in bilateral ties. That thaw is partly driven by United States President Donald Trump’s trade war, which has pushed nuclear-armed rivals Beijing and New Delhi closer.

Yet the alleged Chinese incursions into India underscore how, despite warm handshakes in New Delhi, tensions along the 3,500-kilometre (2,200-mile) border between the neighbours threaten to undercut efforts to normalise ties.

They also pose a major political challenge to Modi, who has built an image as being strong on national security, but who has in recent years faced difficult questions about the relationship with China.

The face-offs with Chinese forces in Arunachal Pradesh – that “still continue”, according to Kapur – come six years after at least 20 Indian troops were killed in hand-to-hand combat with Chinese forces in mountainous Ladakh.

Though satellite imagery and multiple accounts, including from within the Indian security establishment, have since pointed to China effectively taking control of parts of previously disputed territory since that fight, the Modi government has refused to concede that it has given up any land.

And five days after Kapur’s comments on recent standoffs, the Indian government is yet to confirm the nature of the border tensions, instead offering more boilerplate criticisms of China.

Kapur, the ITBP chief, was speaking at a felicitation ceremony for the paramilitary force’s personnel, where he revealed that commandos have been active in the continuing confrontations on the border with China.

Arunachal Pradesh’s remote Upper Subansiri region – where the ongoing face-offs are reported – had seen the first clash between independent India and China in August 1959, which killed at least two Indian soldiers.

Then-Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru spoke of the remoteness of the region in his account of the clash, when he told Parliament that the border post under Chinese attack was roughly three weeks’ march from the nearest roadhead.

The decades-long India-China border dispute is rooted in a British-drawn border, called the McMahon Line. In 1914, British India and Tibet, not under Chinese control at the time, signed the Simla Convention, demarcating their border. Since gaining independence in 1947, India has treated the McMahon Line as its border with China. But China, which came under communist rule in 1949, rejects the line as the boundary with India, arguing that Tibet lacked the authority to conclude the agreement independently.

Beijing claims the entire state of Arunachal Pradesh and refers to it as “South Tibet” or “Zangnan”. China also controls Aksai Chin, a slice of the disputed Kashmir region that India and Pakistan claim in full.

In 1962, India and China agreed to treat the Line of Actual Control (LAC) – meant to acknowledge the actual areas they each control – as their de facto boundary while negotiating their broader border differences.

Those differences were never bridged in the following years, keeping the disputed frontier a persistent flashpoint in relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.

The dispute erupted again into a deadly confrontation in June 2020, when Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Galwan Valley in eastern Ladakh, with both sides accusing the other of crossing the LAC. At least 20 Indian soldiers were killed, and China later acknowledged four deaths among its troops.

Praveen Donthi, a senior analyst at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, said that border tensions amid a thaw in bilateral relations now appear as “part of a pattern” – “likely a pressure tactic by Beijing,” he added.

And due to the undemarcated border, “stand-offs are bound to occur from time to time, some of which may go out of hand”, Donthi warned.

But the 2020 clash also pushed Modi into a corner domestically, as the opposition parties pressured the government over its opaque handling of China. The Modi government also faced opposition complaints over restrictions on parliamentary scrutiny, questions about whether intelligence agencies had detected the Chinese troop build-up, and limited disclosure of operational details.

Contradictions between the government’s own stand and Modi’s claims also prompted accusations that he was trying to minimise – or even hide – the scale of the crisis along the border.

On June 17, 2020, soon after the Galwan clash, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar spoke to his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.

“The Chinese side sought to erect a structure in Galwan Valley on our side of the LAC,” the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said after the phone call. “While this became a source of dispute, the Chinese side took premeditated and planned action that was directly responsible for the resulting violence and casualties. It reflected an intent to change the facts on ground in violation of all our agreements to not change the status quo.”

Yet two days later, Modi said on Twitter, now X, that “neither has anyone been able to enter our territory, nor is anyone still on our territory” – an assertion that disputed the foreign ministry’s account. If no Chinese troops had crossed the LAC, why had Indian soldiers been forced to fight them, the opposition and other strategic analysts asked?

The government has never answered those questions, with Modi’s office only issuing a clarification that the prime minister meant that there were no Chinese troops still in Indian territory after the clash.

Six years since the Ladakh clash, the Chinese incursion has returned to challenge Modi’s strongman image at home – which has already taken a hit from youth-led protests in the country that forced out Modi’s education minister in July this year.

In his address, ITBP chief Kapur also recalled the 2020 clash, outlining a specialised training programme “to better equip personnel to deal with” a Ladakh-like situation.

Kapur, who is due to retire this week, also warned that China’s frontier military capabilities had advanced – and Indian forces may not be able to take a fight head-on by traditional methods.

The Crisis Group’s Donthi said that the Modi government “presents an image of a hard security state with zero tolerance for national security failures”. but “the power differential with China is quite sharp, so it tends to downplay any event that reflects poorly”.

The opposition Congress party’s top leader in Arunachal Pradesh state, Bosiram Siram, said that Chinese troops have intruded nearly 50km (31 miles) deep into Indian territory in remote Upper Subansiri.

A Siram-led party delegation visited border areas in August after initial reports of China’s incursions, and Siram added that “Chinese personnel are stationed up there”, referring to Indian territory.

“You can see the [Chinese] Army. They are on top of the mountains, while we are down below,” Siram added.

In response to the ITBP chief’s remarks, India’s foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that “the situation in India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns”. He did not comment on the ongoing face-offs.

BR Deepak, a professor of Chinese studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) in Delhi, said that the reports of Chinese incursion pose a challenge to Modi’s “credibility and accountability”.

Since 2012, India and China have relied on an official channel that deters border disputes from snowballing, without resolving the underlying question of where their Himalayan boundary lies.

The so-called Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs (WMCC) has officials from both countries and operates alongside military channels.

Its latest round, the 36th WMCC, was held on August 6 – nearly a month after reports of Chinese incursion first emerged in Arunachal Pradesh. In September, a first-ever commander-level meeting was held in Arunachal Pradesh.

Deepak said that “the continuing face-offs show that these diplomatic efforts have not eliminated the friction.” He argued that “meetings at the military or local level can provide temporary relief and help prevent escalation, but they cannot, by themselves, deliver a lasting solution to a border dispute rooted in decades of historical, political and strategic differences”.

And in the absence of “clear political guidance and a coordinated response” in both capitals, Deepak said, any border-level arrangements will “remain fragile and reversible, as seen in [Ladakh] and now in Upper Subansiri in Arunachal Pradesh”.

articles.title: Qatar’s Emir meets Iran’s Pezeshkian in Moscow
articles.summary: The pair discussed energy cooperation and ways to enhance bilateral relations, Iranian state media reported.
articles.body:
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has met Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani on the sidelines of an energy forum in Moscow, Iranian state media reported.

The two leaders “reviewed the current state of relations between Tehran and Doha and emphasised the importance of expanding political and economic relations and utilising existing capacities to enhance the level of bilateral cooperation”, Iranian state television reported on Tuesday.

They also reportedly discussed expanding cooperation in the energy sector at the meeting on the sidelines of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow.

There was no mention of a discussion of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has seen Iran conduct missile and drone strikes on a range of targets across the region, including in Qatar.

Doha has been taking part in mediation efforts to end the nearly eight-month-old war. At a weekly briefing on Tuesday, a foreign ministry spokesman called for Iran to stop threatening Gulf states so that diplomacy can help to defuse tensions in the Middle East.

He added that a Qatari delegation visited Tehran to support mediation efforts and help pave the way for a resolution with the United States.

articles.title: Do you really need an exfoliating body wash? Dermatologists weigh in
articles.summary: Exfoliating body washes help to remove extra dead skin cells that cause acne and dryness — I asked experts whether you actually need one in your routine.
articles.body: Not all body washes work the same, and while most will cleanse dirt and grime from your skin while you shower, many won’t address certain issues like acne, dryness and rough texture. That’s where exfoliating body washes come in: They can help remove dead skin cells, get rid of excess oil and reduce dry patches and bumps. But how do you choose the right one, and how often should you be using it? I asked Dr. Hadley King, a board-certified dermatologist and founder of Hadley King Dermatology in New York City, and board-certified NYC cosmetic dermatologist Dr. Michele Green about everything you need to know when shopping for an exfoliating body wash. I also gathered options I’ve tried myself and recommendations from experts and NBC Selected editors. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. The best exfoliating body washes Best overall Naturium’s viral fragrance-free body wash combines five different alpha hydroxy acids, including glycolic, malic and lactic acids, which gently exfoliate away dead skin. I used it over the summer and loved its creamy texture compared to other harsher exfoliating washes I’ve tried, which made it feel gentle on my sensitive summertime skin. I also love how long the bottle lasts; I use two or three pumps per wash daily and it still lasts me around a month. Best for beginners This is one of our favorite acne body washes, and Green calls it “an excellent starting point for most people,” especially those with sensitive skin. The body wash has salicylic acid and lactic acid to smooth skin, niacinamide to calm any redness or irritation and ceramides to help restore and maintain your skin barrier, she says. It’s also fragrance-free and noncomedogenic, meaning it won’t clog pores. Best for acne This multi-acid body wash comes recommended by Green to help treat dull, flaky skin, which is why we chose it as one of our top 100 acne treatments. It has glycolic, lactic and mandelic acids to clear dirt and bacteria, along with pineapple enzymes to help gently exfoliate. It’s also great for all skin types, but Green warns that the scented formula may not be best for sensitive skin. NBC Selected commerce editor Mili Godio, who’s very prone to back and body acne, says this wash did what others couldn’t: It helped clear her acne without drying out her sensitive skin. “It was hydrating, lightweight and cleared acne by the third week of using it,” she says. Best for sensitive skin Godio’s sensitive skin can sometimes lead to a lot of irritation and redness when using an exfoliant. However, she’s been using this Method body wash for over six months and says it’s one of the only physical exfoliants that isn’t harsh on her skin. It has a mix of physical and chemical exfoliants, like lactic acid and microbeads of bamboo dust. “The beads are super tiny, so they don’t feel too rough, and I can use the body wash every day without worrying about it harming my skin barrier,” says Godio. Best for oily skin Dermatologists recommended this body wash from Necessaire in our guide to acne body washes. It has acne-fighting exfoliants like salicylic acid and has niacinamide to help even out skin tone. It’s also great for oily skin since it helps to regulate sebum production, according to the brand. Best scrub I tested this body wash for our Cyklar brand guide, and although I was skeptical at first, I liked how smooth my skin felt after using it for several weeks. Godio, who also tested the wash, says it helped reduce bumps and texture on her skin after about two weeks. However, we both agree the chemical-like smell isn’t the most pleasant, so we usually follow it up with a scented body wash. Most affordable This Dove body wash, recommended by a board-certified dermatologist in our guide to salicylic acid, is an effective and affordable way to prevent body acne. It has a lightweight gel texture and it’s made with glycerin to keep skin hydrated. Best for keratosis pilaris If you’re focused on smoothing out rough texture and uneven skin tone, Green recommends this body wash for its high concentration of glycolic acid, which helps to exfoliate away bumps. It’s especially great for soothing dry, rough patches from keratosis pilaris. It’s also fragrance- and oil-free, and works for all skin types. Best brightening Medicube’s Kojic Acid Toner is one of my favorite products to reduce dark spots on my back. The body wash version also has kojic acid, turmeric and vitamin C to help brighten skin, along with AHAs (like glycolic acid) to gently exfoliate, according to the brand. It also has niacinamide to soothe and soften skin. How I picked the best exfoliating body washes Here are the key ingredients I kept in mind when choosing the best body washes, based on my experts’ advice: Lactic acid and glycolic acid: These are AHAs that help dissolve and remove dead cells from the surface of your skin, making them great for improving roughness and texture, says King.Salicylic acid: This is a BHA that is oil-soluble, which makes it particularly useful for clogged pores, acne-prone skin and follicular bumps, says King.Urea: The effects of urea depend on how strong the concentration is. At lower concentrations, it helps hydrate; at higher concentrations (usually 30-50%), it has keratolytic properties, which means it helps to shed dead skin and soften thick, rough skin, says King.Poly-hydroxy acids: Known simply as PHAs, these acids (like gluconolactone) are best for sensitive skin because they’re gentler chemical exfoliants, which helps lessen the chances of irritation, says King.Physical exfoliants: More abrasive particles like sugar, jojoba beads or volcanic pumice can manually remove dead skin, says King. However, she generally prefers smooth, non-abrasive particles over coarser scrubs because the latter can irritate skin and even cause more breakouts. Gentler exfoliants usually have very fine beads, and many transition to a cream or foam as the beads are massaged into the skin. Do you need an exfoliating body wash? Since your skin naturally sheds dead skin cells, an exfoliating body wash isn’t technically necessary, says King. “It’s more of a targeted tool than an essential step for everyone,” she says. However, since the skin’s natural shedding process slows with age, it can be a great way to keep your skin smooth and pores clear without adding extra steps to your routine, says Green. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. articles.title: Who are Mizrahis? Netanyahu’s loyal base who may vote for Eisenkot in pivotal polls
articles.summary: Israelis are voting on Tuesday in one of the pivotal elections in the Jewish nation's history, and with much of the voting already done, one question
articles.body: Israelis are voting on Tuesday in one of the pivotal elections in the Jewish nation's history, and with much of the voting already done, one question hangs over the result.Will Mizrahi Jews, long the backbone of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, stay loyal this time? If even a modest share drift away, it could tip the balance towards his challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, who comes from the Mizrahi community.Who are the MizrahiMizrahi Jews are those who came to Israel, mostly in the 1950s, from Arabic-speaking countries across the Middle East and North Africa. Many met discrimination from the European-descended, or Ashkenazi, elites who have traditionally dominated government, the military and business.Over the decades, many Mizrahi families came to identify with the right and with Likud in particular. Voting for the party became a matter of identity as much as ideology. That history gives this election an unusual edge as Israel has never had a Mizrahi prime minister.Eisenkot, 66, a former army chief and the son of Moroccan immigrants, could be the first. He grew up in Tiberias and Eilat, far from the centres of power, and he rarely speaks about his heritage.A remark that forced the issueIn the final days of the campaign, his background was pushed into the open. Yinon Magal, a prominent television host widely seen as a mouthpiece for Netanyahu, called Eisenkot a “monkey” of “a Mizrahi-Moroccan” heritage managed by “Ashkenazi elites”. The words touched a raw nerve and set off a political and media storm.Magal later said he had not meant to mock Eisenkot’s ethnic origins. He said he was using an underworld term for a frontman who is controlled from behind the scenes. Even Netanyahu, not known for contrition, condemned the remarks. For a prime minister who relies on Mizrahi loyalty, that was a sign of how sensitive the subject has become.Cracks in a loyal baseThe real test lies in places such as Qiryat Shemona, Israel’s northernmost city. In the elections of 2021 and 2022, around half of its voters chose Likud, compared with about a quarter nationwide.The town is overwhelmingly Mizrahi and has been battered by the conflict with Hezbollah. It was evacuated for more than a year, and many residents say Netanyahu has not delivered the security he promised.Eti Ben Shabat, 64, says she once voted Likud almost without thinking, following her family. This time she backed Eisenkot.“I don’t want the lies to continue,” she said. Her choice was not easy in a close-knit community where there is pressure to vote a certain way. “It’s a small place, so people aren’t speaking about it openly,” she said. “But inside, people really want a change,” she told PBS News.The numbers point the same way. A poll for Agam Labs at Hebrew University found support for Netanyahu across northern Israel falling from around 29 per cent before the 2022 election to around 17 per cent this month.Why the outcome is still openDisillusion with Netanyahu does not automatically mean votes for Eisenkot. Nimrod Nir, who directs Agam Labs, expects most frustrated Likud voters to move to hardline parties such as Otzma Yehudit and the Religious Zionist Party. Those parties would probably back Netanyahu as prime minister, but they would hold greater power inside his coalition.Eisenkot’s position is strong but not decisive. Most recent polls projected his Yashar party at 20 to 23 of the 120 Knesset seats, ahead of Likud. Neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the anti-Netanyahu bloc appear on course for the 61 seats needed for a majority, so deadlock remains possible.That is why small shifts could matter the most as a dip in support in Likud’s traditional strongholds could hand Eisenkot a narrow edge.A move to the far right could leave Netanyahu in office on harder terms. Either way, the Mizrahi vote has rarely counted for more.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ballon d'Or ceremony raises case of French sports journalist Christophe Gleizes jailed in Algeria
articles.summary: He is in jail accused of supporting terrorism after travelling to the politically sensitive region Kabylie.
articles.body:
The plight of French sports journalist Christophe Gleizes, who is serving a seven-year prison sentence in Algeria, was highlighted at the Ballon d'Or ceremony.

Run by France Football magazine, the prestigious football awards were held in London where presenters Kate Scott and Thierry Henry dedicated the occasion to the 37-year-old reporter.

On a large screen behind them, it stated that he had been in jail for one year, three months and 27 days and alongside his photo was the hashtag "#FreeGleize".

He was arrested on a trip to Algeria where he had gone to report on a football club in Kabylie, a region where some people want self-determination. The authorities accused him of supporting terrorism.

"The Ballon d'Or France Football family would like to take this opportunity to dedicate this ceremony to Christophe Gleizes," said British broadcaster Scott and former Arsenal player and French striker Henry as the ceremony kicked off on Monday evening.

The event, held in London for the first time in its 70-year history, saw England and Bayern Munich strike Harry Kane crowned the world's top footballer of the year and London's City's Spanish midfielder Alexia Putellas taking the female prize.

Kane ends England's 25-year Ballon d'Or wait - how he bucked the trend

Putellas wins record-equalling third Ballon d'Or

Gleizes, who contributes to French magazines So Foot and Society, travelled to Algeria in May 2024 to report on Jeunesse Sportive de Kabylie (JSK), one of the country's best-known football clubs.

It is based in Tizi Ouzou, about 100km (62 miles) east of the capital Algiers, in the mountainous Kabylie region, which is mainly home to the ethnic Amazigh people (historically known as Berbers).

It is also the base of the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylie (MAK), which Algeria designated a terrorist organisation in 2021.

Gleizes was accused of possessing publications deemed harmful to national security.

The case centred on his contacts with a JSK official who was also associated with the MAK.

Reporters Without Borders (RSF), which has campaigned for his release, says the exchanges took place in a journalistic context and that some contacts predated the outlawing of the group.

During his appeal hearing last December, Gleizes acknowledged mistakes in his reporting and said he should have applied for a journalist visa rather than entering Algeria on a tourist visa.

"I beg your mercy so that I can be reunited with my family," he told the court.

Prosecutors argued that he had not travelled to Algeria to carry out journalistic work, but to commit a hostile act.

The Algerian authorities have yet to commented on the decision by the Ballon d'Or, which is organised by France Football magazine in partnership with European football governing body Uefa, to dedicate the ceremony to Gleizes.

RSF has announced a solidarity football match for 11 November, marking Gleizes's 500th day in detention, as part of its campaign calling for his release.

Former France internationals Robert Pirès and Vikash Dhorasoo, along with Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire, are among the first participants announced.

Gleizes's case comes amid wider concerns over the prosecution and imprisonment of writers and other public figures in Algeria.

Franco-Algerian writer Boualem Sansal was sentenced to five years in prison for undermining national security before receiving a pardon from President Abdelmadjid Tebboune following mediation by Germany's president in 2025.

Gleizes's arrest also came during a period of heightened diplomatic tensions between France and Algeria, marked by the withdrawal of ambassadors and reciprocal expulsions of diplomats.

Relations deteriorated further after France recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in July 2024. Algeria supports the pro-independence Polisario Front, which seeks independence for the disputed territory.

As relations began to improve in May, France's Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin visited Algiers and urged the Algerian authorities to allow Gleizes to reunite "not with France, but with his mother".

He said that he believed President Tebboune would be receptive to the request.

articles.title: Complete construction of exhibits at science city by 2028: CM
articles.summary: Bihar CM Samrat Choudhary sets 2028 deadline for Science City exhibits in Patna, reviews Rs 100cr+ projects, NH-119D target 2027 and housing schemes.
articles.body: Patna: Chief minister Samrat Choudhary on Tuesday directed officials to complete the construction of exhibits for various galleries at Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Science City in Patna here by 2028, saying the project must advance scientific temper, innovation and science education in Bihar. The science city is located in Rajendra Nagar, and officials were told to coordinate across departments for their completion.The instruction came during a review of state projects costing more than Rs 100 crore each monitored under “Bihar Gati” and the central govt schemes. The meeting was held at Sankalp auditorium in Lok Sevak Awas. Choudhary asked departments to accelerate implementation of development works, follow prescribed timelines and ensure that welfare benefits reach eligible beneficiaries.Reviewing the 55-km Amas-Shivrampur section in Package-1 of Amas-Darbhanga route under NH-119D, Choudhary said the stretch should be completed by 2027. He also directed officials to proceed with the required agreement with National Highways Authority of India under the Bihar Reservoir Restoration and Silt Management Policy to enable effective implementation of related works.On Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Gramin), the CM ordered faster completion of the housing survey and speedy, transparent disposal of objections so that eligible families receive assistance on time. He said the target of constructing 12 lakh houses under the rural housing scheme should be achieved soon, with flood-affected families placed on the priority list.During the review of Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Mahaabhiyan (PM-JANMAN), the focus was on providing pucca houses to eligible families from Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups. Choudhary directed officials to run a special campaign so that tribal families can access the scheme’s benefits.He also reviewed land availability for beneficiaries seeking house construction support under Mukhyamantri Vas Sthal Kray Sahayata Yojana. District secretaries in charge were told to conduct circle-wise assessments of govt land availability and take steps to resolve difficulties in extending assistance. While assessing Mukhyamantri Gramin Awas Yojana, Choudhary instructed officials to monitor implementation regularly and ensure benefits are provided as per prescribed provisions.The CM said govt was committed to completing projects within deadlines and taking welfare benefits to the person at the last rung. articles.title: King Charles’s Caribbean tour: Will he discuss slavery reparations?
articles.summary: UK’s King Charles launches nine-day Caribbean tour amid monarchy questions and growing demands for slavery reparations.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom’s King Charles lll is travelling to the Bahamas on Tuesday, where he will begin a nine-day tour of the Caribbean.

The tour will take him to the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda, where he will attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) from November 1-4.

This comes as demands for reparations over Britain’s notorious role in the slave trade grow louder, and as the monarchy faces questions about its future in the region.

So what is the significance of this tour? And what does the Caribbean want?

King Charles will visit three countries in nine days.

His tour begins on Tuesday with the archipelagic country of the Bahamas, where he will be staying for three days.

Then he will make his way to Guyana, a former British colony that had more than 100,000 slaves when the trade was abolished in 1807.

After two days in Guyana, where he is expected to meet the president and elected leaders of Amerindian villages, he will head to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

The meeting, from November 1-4, is expected to include discussions about the environment and trade and development, although the question of British reparations for slavery is also likely to feature.

What do the countries King Charles is visiting want?

Government officials in the Bahamas and in Antigua and Barbuda – both of which are part of the British Commonwealth with King Charles as their ultimate head of state – have signalled that they want to become republics. Guyana gained independence from the UK in 1966, and has a president as its head of state.

Guyanese President Mohamed Irfaan Ali said in an interview with ITV News that while Charles “rightfully” recognised slavery as the “darkest days in human history” during a visit to Barbados in 2021 when he was still the prince of Wales, an apology should be his next step.

“You exploited the region. You destroyed lives. You created underdevelopment,” Ali said, in a reference to the lingering legacy of the British Empire and the slave trade.

In 2023, a Lord Ashcroft Poll revealed that 51 percent of surveyed respondents in the Bahamas wanted to become a republic, while 27 percent preferred to retain the British monarchy as head of state.

Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee, was critical of the king ahead of his arrival. “Why do we still have a king? What does this person really represent to us? Why is he coming and how will that benefit us?” she asked.

What do other countries in the Caribbean say about slavery?

Jamaica , which is not on the itinerary for this trip by King Charles, made its stance clear in September, when it filed a $10bn slavery reparations petition in London, addressing it to the king.

That was the first time a British Commonwealth state has taken legal action pursuing “the cause of reparatory justice”, as the Jamaican delegation called it.

The petition is due to be heard by a UK privy council in March next year. The UK has, so far, refused to formally apologise or pay reparations for slavery.

Also in September, Caribbean Community and Common Market (CARICOM) Secretary-General Carla Barnett said reparations are “fundamentally about justice”.

“It is about recognition, accountability and transformation, and about building a just and equitable future for the descendants of those who, as the chattel of colonial owners, endured untold suffering, loss of life and freedom,” she said.

The transatlantic slave trade was recently declared the “gravest crime against humanity” in a United Nations resolution in March this year.

The last time a British royal visited Jamaica was when Prince William and Kate Middleton, then the duke and duchess of Cambridge, toured the island in 2022 during their Caribbean Platinum Jubilee tour.

The more memorable moment of the trip was when the couple was pictured shaking hands with Jamaican children with a fence separating them, which many criticised for being “tone-deaf”.

What’s likely to happen at the Commonwealth meeting?

The meeting in Antigua and Barbuda is expected to cover climate resilience as well as trade and development.

Leaders and representatives of 56 Commonwealth countries will be attending. Many want an apology for slavery from the king, but Buckingham Palace recently announced that will not be happening.

“The visit programme will…not shy away from ‘the darkest days of our past’, as his majesty has described them, but – in keeping with the wishes of our host nations – ‌it ⁠will principally be oriented to the vibrant present and promising future of each country,” a palace spokesperson said in a statement.

The palace added that it is “important” to acknowledge the “creative” ways that Charles has tried to right “enduring inequalities”.

The chair of the UK’s All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, said the royal family and the UK government had failed to recognise the demands of those wanting reparations.

“I think it would be wrong to think that we can continue with platitudes. You’ve got ‘atrocity’, ‘deep regret’, ‘sorrow’, and now they’re going to say ‘darkest days’,” she said. “I think the king needs to realise that people wouldn’t keep raising it if what he was doing was anywhere near enough.

“You can tell that the Commonwealth means something to the monarchy, and I’m sure he would not want to be the monarch under which it crumbles.”
